Abstract
The service oriented architecture is a widely used con-
cept to construct the web applications. Among several im-
plementations, the bus model is proposed to coordinate het-
erogeneous services. However, it is difﬁcult to analyze the
properties of the composition pattern using buses in prac-
tice. Therefore, it is extremely necessary to provide a theo-
retical foundation for it. In this paper, we focus on the spec-
iﬁcation of services in the bus system and the properties of
their parallel executions. The service model is formalized
on three levels and a composition approach is proposed to
describe the composition pattern with the bus infrastruc-
ture. The idea of separating the communication from the
computation gives the model more ﬂexibility.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: With the development of Web Service technologies [1], enterprise applications are encapsulated as services. For that reason, an infrastructure is needed for managing so many transactions involving service consumptions. How to integrate existing services and how to expand their capa- bilities easily have become essential issues. Moreover, ser- vices are usually acquired from the Internet, which means the users only get the brief specifications of services. The internal implementation details are unobservable. So many years have been taken to seek an appropriate and flexible model for the service coordination. The Service Oriented Architecture (SOA) [7] is one of the approaches developed to solve the problem. Recently, it has received increasing attention by the industry since it acts well in the enterprise environment. Furthermore, the bus model which is based on SOA concept comes to the front. The bus model does a good job in dealing with most of the coordination issues including the management of control flow and data flow, communication patterns and security aspects. A con- crete application of bus model is known as Enterprise Ser- vice Bus (ESB) [5]. The significance of ESB is reflecting the enterprise needs which include the manageability, flexibility and integrabil- ity in a heterogeneous environment. Enlighten by the ESB, we abstract a general bus model having the following basic capabilities.[12]. ! Communication The bus provides the interaction interface for services and routes the messages services want to exchange with each other. It also unifies transport protocols and messaging styles to provide a widely available messag- ing platform for heterogeneous services. ! Integration The bus provides the transformation service which en- titles the services using heterogeneous protocols to in- teract with each other freely. The integration patterns make it easy for service substitutions. ! Service Interaction The bus separates the specification of services from their implementation. It requires the service interface definition and service messaging model. The substi- tution of service implementation is supported without changing other aspects. ! Management and Autonomy The bus centralizes the control and distributes the pro- cessing. An administration capability is needed with the autonomic execution without user interferences. It manages control flow and data flow but leaves the pro- cessing details to the client services. We intend to develop a formal model to describe the ca- pabilities of the bus infrastructure. This paper mainly con- centrates on the specification of client services and the def- inition of the bus composition pattern. sections.heading: Figure 2. The formalization of service compo-
sections.text: sition based on buses [10, 2] and CCS [15, 16]. They use the concept of chan- nels to simulate the process communications and synchro- nize process executions. However, as we learned in our for- mer works [13, 14], the channel model may not be flexible enough to express interactions between services in a large scale distributed environment such as a bus system. The be- havior of the whole bus system is also hard to be depicted using channels. As shown in Fig. 1, given five services, four channels will be needed for each service. If there are n services, the number of channels they need is n ( n − 1) 2 . If some modification is made on the channels of a single ser- vice, the change may force substituting n − 1 channel names in the definition of other services, which is obviously inflex- ible. Although multi-ends channels will avoid this problem, but the management for the multi-ends channels raises other problems. The representation is also more complex, which is against our expects. Fig. 2 depicts the rough concept of the bus infrastructure. The bus model has some advantages compared with the channel model. For instance, the com- munications between services in the bus system are asyn- chronous by default. The execution of a service can be more independent by requiring less information about other ser- vices. The bus composition is more suitable for describing the true concurrency of services in a distributed environ- ment. The interactions in the bus system are similar to Linda [8, 3]. Linda is a coordination language that coordinates the interactions among distributed agents. Agents get tu- ples from a tuple space and put tuples into it to meet their communication needs. Recently, Linda has been improved in many aspects [6, 4]. However, the extensions burden the semantical analysis of the system behavior. In this paper, the behavior of the bus system is embodied by the contributions of its client services. Services can be described in a three-level model. On the first level, the pred- icate calculus is used to specify the computation behavior of services. A service is described by its requirement and contribution. Level 2 extends the service on level 1 by in- troducing a local space to store the values. The third level describes communications between services and the bus in- frastructure. Since the communication is separated from the computation, the model can support multiple communica- tion patterns than CCS or CSP. In our formalization, the function of the bus is abstracted to store and update the values of the shared variables among services. It provides a global space like the tuple space in Linda for the services to access and modify in order to re- alize the coordination in a distributed computation environ- ment. A denotational semantical model for the services exe- cuting in the bus environment is made to analyze the behav- ior of a bus system composed by the services. The model is enlightened by the Unifying Theories of Programming [11] and some of its applications [9, 17]. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Sec- tion 2 formalizes the computation behavior of services with the predicate model. It forms the first level of the service specification. Section 3 defines the level 2 and level 3 model of the service communication behavior. Section 4 mainly refers to the service composition in the bus system. The system provides a parallel execution environment for ser- vices. Given services we defined in the three-level model, the denotational semantics of the composition is proposed concisely. Some examples are also given to demonstrate the analysis of the system behavior. Finally, Section 5 con- cludes the paper and states the future work. 2

sections.heading: Services Computation Model
sections.text: A bus consists of some client services and a shared space supporting their communications. Some constraints need to be imposed in order to enable the services to be the client of buses, whatever the services used to be. A services consists of two kinds of behaviors: the com- putation behavior and the communication behavior. In nor- mal cases, the service can start up with some kind of input and then make the computation in reference to the input. The computation will produce some results when it is done. In summary, the computation behavior of the service can be specified by something like the Hoare Logic which can be represented with predicates. The computation behavior can be divided into atomic programs. Each program’s semantics can be defined as a conceptual predicate, which restricts the variables involved in the computation.

sections.heading: Service Communication Model
sections.text: Together with the computation behavior, the communi- cation behavior includes sending and receiving messages. Particularly in a bus system, services register their charac- ters to the bus and exchange information through it. The bus system coordinates the executions of the services by means of invoking them with messages and obtaining their contri- butions. In our formalization, messages are considered as a list of name-value pairs denoting the information. The bus has the messages stored in its shared space which is acces- sible for all its clients. We hold the assumption that two or more acquisitions involve the same variable if their names are the same. Moreover, a variable has only one value at a moment. Then the messages can form a space which con- tains all the name-value pairs appearing in the messages. The consumption of the messages can be considered as the access to the space. Formally, a space Σ can be defined as function from vari- able to value. Σ : V ariable → V alue where V ariable is a set of names of variables and V alue is a set of value. In the following part, we use the space concept to substitute the messages. 3.1

sections.heading: Extending Model with Local Space
sections.text: In our model, we assume that a service does not commu- nicate with the environment during its computation process. The motivation of this design is to guarantee the atomic ex- ecution. It will be a disaster when a data obtained by a service is modified by another service during the computa- tion. In order to avoid the problem, the data involved in the computation should be stored in a local space so that only the local program can modify the values. In this way, every service has an uninterrupt computation behavior. Every service has its own local space. Its computation behavior uses the values in the local space and generates 290 Authorized licensed use limited to: University of Lancashire. As the program variables men- tioned in the program model, the local space can be denoted by two variables in the Σ type: π storing the variables with the initial value and π ′ containing the final values of vari- ables after the execution. The notation π (˜ x ) represents the values of the variables ˜ x in the subspace π and π ′ (˜ x ) gets the values in subspace π ′ . This kind of program with a local space is called agent in the paper.

sections.heading: Space
sections.text: In the bus system, the bus has its own space. It can be considered as a global space for the client services. Ser- vices get the values from the shared bus space to their local spaces and put their results to the bus space to update the environment. A service has the capability to operate its own local space and the global bus spaces. The local space and the global space are depicted in Fig. 3. In the service registration, the global bus space creates a set of variables collected from the characters declared by the client services. The free vari- ables in any service’s local space is contained in the global space. When a service finishes its computation, it should write the values of free variables back to the global space so that the following services can access the updated val- ues. This mechanism not only avoids the outside influence of the execution but also enables the services to exchange 291 Authorized licensed use limited to: University of Lancashire. Downloaded on October 28,2026 at 14:50:01 UTC from IEEE Xplore. Restrictions apply. the information. We use σ to represent the shared data space where the values of all the free variables of the clients are stored. Ser- vices can access or modify the space before or after their computation behaviors. A service S can be defined as S := true ∗ ( S.get (˜ x ); S.SA P ; S.put (˜ x )) S is defined as an iteration since the service is always run- ning. SA P is the agent model with extended state variables which we will discuss later. Just like the agent, SA P has the property that P � α, β � , which means the function aspect of the service is determined by its character. Two commands get and put are added to the definition to endow the ser- vice with the capability to acquire and publish information through the bus space. The notation S. added in all the pro- grams is introduced for distinguishing the programs belong- ing to different services. Consider a service S with its P satisfying P � α, β � . The values are copied form the global space σ by get command when they can trigger the α condition. Since its local space π is filled with the values which satisfy its requirement, the following computation is done by SA P within the service. When the computation is finished successfully, the values in the local space are actually the results of the service which satisfy the β condition of the service. In order to analyze the execution state of the service, we extend the state variable we introduced when we discuss the programs. The states of the services can help the bus infrastructure to coordinate the execution of the services and support a choreography. Concretely, we extend the range of state variable’s value to the following ones: ! complete: a service is in this complete state if one of its execution circle is successfully done. ! run: the state represents the service is executing its computation behavior. ! wait: denotes the wait state. The service is waiting for appropriate condition of the environment. It occurs in the execution of the get command. ! submit: When the service finishes its computation be- havior successfully, it will enter this submit state in which it provides the updated values intending to mod- ify the environment. ! div: Generally speaking, the divergence will not occur in the service model since the the get command can guarantee the requirement of the computation behav- ior. But it can also be triggered in the iteration when the boolean condition can never be met. In this paper we assume the local program is robust that the diver- gence is unreachable. Therefore, we remove the div state from the original value set of the state variables.

sections.heading: Figure 4. The transformation of the service
sections.text: state observed by the environment The transformation of the service state is depicted in Fig. 4. The transformation (1) will occur when the environment can provide sufficient information and the service executes the get command successfully. If the requirement is not met, the transformation (2) causes the state to be wait . The wait state will turn to run only if the environment is up- dated to satisfy the service’s α , which is denoted by the the transformation (3). Then the service executes its computa- tion behavior until reaches the submit state. If the service can complete the transformation (4), it means that the com- putation is successful and the new values of the free vari- ables stored in the local space are ready for being written back to the environment. If the operation causes no con- flicts, it will be done immediately and if other service also want to update the same variable, the updating order is non- deterministic. Finally, the service will complete its updating and the state will become complete represented by (5). In this paper, we use ψ to represent the shared state space in the bus and define ψ ( S i .st ) to get the state value of S i . In the initialization, all the state variables in the global state space are mapped to complete . The state variable in the global state space has some dif- ferences with the local state variable. The local state vari- able is introduced in the semantical model which is invisible to the environment. The one in the global state space is just like the data variable which can be observed by the environ- ment. The services interact with the bus space with their get and put commands. sections.heading: Service Composition Through Buses
sections.text: Based on the three-level model of the services, we have a method to describe the behavior of the service compo- sition through buses. A bus system can be defined as the parallel composition of the services. The communications between the services are achieved by the bus infrastructure which consists of a global data space and state space to ob- serve the execution state of the services and coordinate the modification of the global data space by the services. In syntax, a bus system can be represented as follows: B ::= ≀≀ n i =1 ( S i ) where the notation ≀≀ denotes the special composition pat- tern in the bus system where the services connects to the bus infrastructure and yields its coordination. The behavior of a bus system can be represented by all the contributions of the client services and their execution states. The contributions can be observed with the changing of the global data space and the global state space. In our definition of the services in level 3 model, a service has a finite trace to record the situation of the global bus spaces from initialization to a certain observation time. This trace is open to all of the services so that it can record all of their contributions. In the local view, every service has a trace to record the whole system’s behavior. In the global view, these traces recorded by all the services is totally identical if they describe the same execution process of the bus system. Therefore, the composition of the services of the level 3 model can be defined in the following way

In our formalization, the main mechanism for service co- ordination can be concluded as follows. ! All the services can access the global spaces and mod- ify it by publishing their contributions. Services in a bus system do not interact with each other directly. In- stead, they exchange the information through the bus spaces. The mechanism makes the services low cou- pling with each other and provides a platform for them to conform to the given choreography. ! Since the data is obtained from the global data space, a mechanism is required for avoiding the inconsistency caused by others’ modification when the data is pro- cessed by a service. The local space is introduced into the model to solve the problem. When a service needs some data from the global space, a copy of the data is delivered to the service’s local space. The service only deals with the data in its local space until it publishes the results to the global space for return. ! When two or more services intend to update the same variable in the global space, it is forbidden that the new value of the same variable is contributed by differ- ent services. sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The paper has proposed a formal model for services and their compositions through the bus infrastructure. The for- malization of the service model consists of three levels. The main idea which separates the communication behav- ior from the computation behavior produces the flexibility of the formal model. Having the formalization of services, a service compo- sition approach is proposed to construct a bus system. The default asynchronous communication pattern in the bus sys- tem has its advantages in describing the interactions of ser- vices in a distributed environment. The behavior of a bus system can be considered as the true concurrency of in- dependent services. The behavior of the bus system is in- cluded in a trace set whose elements satisfy the denotational semantics of the bus system. Mechanisms including global and local spaces and open traces solve the concurrency con- trol issues, particularly in dealing with the simultaneous modifications of the shred variables. The model we have developed in this paper formalizes a bus infrastructure which supports the minimum capabilities including communication, service interaction, management and autonomy. The integration capability can be easily achieved by adding additional transformation functions to the service model. The next step of our work will introduce the message queue model to the system so that it can support the concrete interaction protocols such as publish/subscribe paradigm. Secondly, an approach will be figured out to automatically divide the complex services into the ones belonging to our three level model. Moreover, the intelligent routing mechanism of ESB is also worthy to research.
